etymologies.heading: Etymology
paragraphs: Coined by Edmund Spenser in 1596 in "blatant beast". Probably a variation of *blatand (Scots blaitand (“bleating”)), present participle of blate, a variation of bleat, equivalent to blate +‎ -ant. See bleat. In addition, it is suggested by Latin blatiō (“speak like a fool, prate”), which is rare, and so the similitude may be just coincidental.
Compare typologically Bulgarian въпие́щ (văpiéšt), Russian вопию́щий (vopijúščij) (akin to вопи́ть (vopítʹ)).
senses: Obvious, on show; unashamed; loudly obtrusive or offensive.
(archaic) Bellowing; disagreeably clamorous; sounding loudly and harshly.
